Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

51.2% of Fulton County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 51.2% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 22.3% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Flood zonePolicy unitsShare
Zone X1,59248.7%
Zone AE (high-risk)1,42543.6%
Zone A (high-risk)2497.6%
Other low-risk or unclassified zones20.1%

Policy records keep the code they were rated with, so older labels such as A1 to A30 are counted on their own. Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk; A1 to A30 and AE are the same kind of area (44 CFR §64.3).

Insured units by the zone each policy is rated in. How this is counted What each means: zone AE, zone X, zone VE.

Flood map: FEMA's current flood map for unincorporated Fulton County took effect September 18, 2013. FEMA's latest Community Status Book lists no new flood map taking effect for the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county; that does not cover maps still preliminary (below). FEMA's digital flood map for Fulton County has 178 map panels, the oldest in effect since September 18, 2013 and the newest since June 19, 2020. FEMA has revised that map by 8 Letters of Map Revision, 5 of them in effect since January 1, 2021. FEMA's map service lists 604 rulings for owners here who asked FEMA to take a building or lot out of the high-risk zone (Letters of Map Amendment): 376 took the building or some or all of the lot out, 90 found it already outside the zone as mapped, 70 were denied, 68 other or mixed. FEMA charges no review or processing fee for a Letter of Map Amendment request (44 CFR §72.5). FEMA's Online LOMC site lets home owners or their representatives ask FEMA for a Letter of Map Change. Your home may already have an Elevation Certificate on file with your community: ask your local floodplain manager, often in the city or county building, permitting or engineering department. If none is on file, a land surveyor, engineer or architect completes one. Rulings for owners who applied (not your home's odds; FEMA's map service gives no dates for them), counted by the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county, so a city that reaches into a neighboring county counts in full here. FEMA's preliminary flood map data give an early look at a home's or community's projected flood risk and may include new or revised flood maps. Check your own address on FEMA's flood map or with our flood zone map lookup by address.

Flood insurance cost in Fulton County, Georgia

In Fulton County, typically about $872 a year ($73 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $591 and $1,264. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $591 · Typical $872 · A quarter pay over $1,264 · A tenth pay $1,919 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 1,860 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Renting? See what renters pay.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Does homeowners insurance cover flooding? To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Wait exceptions, exclusions, premium increases and surcharges, aid, appeals, rebuilding and closing rules: the NFIP rules in full.

Your state's insurance regulator: Georgia Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Fulton County, Georgia: what floods pay out

Floods in Fulton County have led to 3,002 NFIP flood claims and $94.3 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2009, 2024 and 2004.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2009 ($38,660,217), 2024 ($19,208,807), 2004 ($14,847,869). Total paid $94,345,036. Totals for 2025 and 2026 are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

Outside the high-risk zones: of the 593 claims here with a flood zone on the claim, losses 2016–2025, 38.3% were rated outside zones A and V (zones X, B, C and D), and they got 14.5% of the dollars paid on those claims. The zone is the one on each claim, not today's map; claims with no zone on them are left out.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 63.8% of the 1,167 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 1,167 policies reporting one)63.8%Georgia: 38.9%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)82.6%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 2,328 claims paid with a damage figure)2.7%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 14, 2026.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

From about $709 a year (Zone X) to $1,269 (Zone AE) here. Your zone is on your lender's flood determination or FEMA's map; find its row below.

Flood zoneMedian / yrPriced policies
Zone X$7091,098

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

How Fulton County appears in the national research papers

Each paper measures one thing in FEMA's records for every U.S. county with enough records. A fifth is a position in a list, not a grade or a prediction.

  • Flood damage over building coverage: NFIP claims by county: 2.5% (90% range 1.4–4.2%) of 364 paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage here, the middle fifth of 268 U.S. counties listed.
  • Outside the zone: paid flood claims rated outside high-risk zones: 32.6% (90% range 29.2–36.2%) of 485 claims with a payment and a rated zone here, the second fifth of 364 U.S. counties listed.
  • Building deductibles on record: NFIP single-family homes by county: 14.7% (90% range 13.4–16.1%) of 1,853 single-family primary-home policy units with a known building deductible here, the fourth fifth of 1,793 U.S. counties listed.
  • Peak month of NFIP claims by county: 45.9% (90% range if claims were independent 42.5–49.2%) of 593 NFIP claims with a month of loss here, the fourth fifth of 416 U.S. counties listed; peak month September, over half of it from September 2024 alone; 10.3% would be expected at random for this many claims, and the fifth is by share minus that.
  • The gap to FEMA's full-risk premium: NFIP single-family homes by county: 23.2% (90% range 21.7–24.9%) of 1,860 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways here, the fourth fifth of 1,793 U.S. counties listed.

How much flood risk is here?

Relatively High for inland (river) flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Inland flood risk rating (FEMA)Relatively High

FEMA's rating weighs modeled loss with social vulnerability and community resilience; it is not a prediction for your home, and it can differ from the loss percentile below. Inland: FEMA models roughly $164.3 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: inland flood loss here is higher than in about 26% of U.S. counties. Loss figures model all flood loss, insured or not, so they run far above insurance payouts. How this is counted

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI December 2025 release; retrieved November 14, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $10.5 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $1,856 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 14, 2026.
